rationale: Machines that automatically carry out calculus match the differential analyzer's function. The quote gives no mechanism.
A mechanical globe that computes distances is a calculating device but not an equation-solving analog machine. It only loosely points at the differential analyzer.
A machine that performs integration matches the differential analyzer's function. The mechanism is vague and the claimed power is exaggerated.
An MIT integrating machine solving large equation problems closely echoes the Bush analyzer's function. The quote is vague on mechanism and says it was already built by 1929.
A 'similacrum' of a person points toward a person-copy robot, but the quote gives almost nothing about how it works.
Quick-made duplicates of a person are evocative of person copies, but the fading memory impression is a different mechanism from a teleoperated android.
A humandroid built to look and talk exactly like a specific famous person matches the person-copy function. The mechanism is not described.
An electronic duplicate that stands in for a person socially matches the stand-in function of a person-copy android. The quote has no mechanism.
An android double of a man works in his place and is controlled by its maker, which matches the stand-in function. The mechanism of the control is vague.
An android duplicate of a specific human matches the function, though the quote emphasizes autonomous abilities rather than a teleoperated double.
Only a replica city is stated in the quote. It points loosely toward duplication but not to a robot copy of a person.
A remotely run electronic proxy of a specific person matches the teleoperated android double. The context (a revenge plot) differs.
A robot dupe of a human is in the right direction, but it is an autonomous spy unaware of its nature, unlike a teleoperated copy.
A humanoid robot with the original owner's features matches the look-alike function. The mind transplant mechanism differs from teleoperation.
Roboids built as remote-controlled stand-ins for a specific person closely match a teleoperated android copy. The context is fictional impersonation.
A perfect human replica robot with a copied brain pattern matches the copy function. The mechanism (brain transfer) differs from teleoperation.
Android bodies operated by remote control by a human as public stand-ins match the teleoperation mechanism. The quote does not say they duplicate the operator's appearance.
A device making practical androids that copy a person matches the function. The mechanism is only a named gadget.
A physically identical duplicate android of a specific person matches the function. The recorded-mind mechanism is not teleoperation.
An android double of its owner with remote controls matches the teleoperated copy and its key mechanism. It also carries a recorded mind, which differs from the real case.
An android duplicate of a named person used to impersonate him matches the function. The mechanism is not described.
A lifelike robot made in a specific woman's image matches the function. The quote shows a companion doll with no mechanism.
Android duplicates of workers made from a likeness and used as stand-ins match the function, with no mechanism given.
A robot carrying its creator's mind is an evocative copy, but no physical double of the person is stated.
A humanoid robot double impersonating a particular man matches the function, with no mechanism given.
An android that duplicates a specific human exactly matches the function. The mechanism is not described.
A robot that is a magnified version of its creator is only loosely a copy of a person, and it is meant to surpass him.
Androids that duplicate specific individuals match the function, with no mechanism given.
An android self that is a duplicate of a person matches the function, with no mechanism given.
A brain with neuron-like circuits between cells is evocative of neural networks. It arises naturally and has no learning or computing mechanism.
The quote only says the best pattern would be the human brain. It points toward brain-modelled computing but loosely.
A superhuman problem-solving machine suggests a thinking computer. Nothing here describes interconnected neuron-like units or learning.
Mechanical glands and fluid pumping are brain-like but unrelated to neuron-unit computing, so the match is only evocative.
Radioactive pyramidal cells hint at neuron-like computing units, but there is no network or learning mechanism.
A mechanical cortex of billions of electronic cells matches the function of many neuron-like units. The mechanism of learning is missing.
A machine with two nerve-cell equivalents showing lifelike behavior matches a small neuron-unit network. Learning is not stated.
A brain-scale count of synapses is evocative of a neural network, but memory by notched molecules is a different mechanism.
Circuits imitating nerve tissue function in simple robots are in the right direction, but there are no interconnected units that learn.
A compact brain made of neuron-like components is loosely suggestive of a neural network, with no learning or mechanism.
A glass-tube brain filled with nerve fluid is brain-like but a different mechanism from computed neuron units.
A walk-in artificial brain is a vague gesture toward brain-modelled machines only.
Artificial nerves wired to sensors and learned sounds match learning in a neuron-like network. The mechanism is vague and not the Perceptron's.
Pumping nerve fluid into an artificial brain is only loosely suggestive of a neural network.
The quote only reports an expensive man-made brain sitting idle. It points toward artificial brains loosely.
Computers that are electronic analogues of living brains suggest brain-modelled computing, but there are no units or learning.
A machine with sensitive organs acting independently is in the area of machine sensing. It describes an autonomous mind rather than an odour or touch sensor.
Machines given an ear, an eye and a brain are evocative of artificial senses, but they are not touch, taste or smell.
Photo-electric eyes seeing beyond human range involve vision, not smell or touch, so the match is loose.
A robot dowsing sense is an extra artificial sense in a loose way, but it is not chemical sensing of odour.
Taste sensors on a robot for tasting food match the chemical-sensing function. The mechanism is not given.
Distress signals from a warm joint are a loose analogue of touch sensors, with no relation to an electronic nose.
A machine whose senses include detecting the smell of a room matches artificial olfaction in function, with no mechanism stated.
Eye-lenses and ear-drums that trigger distress calls are an evocative sensing idea, but not smell or touch.
Hearing beyond human range is in the concept's scope but far from the electronic nose milestone.
Nose sensors that judge ripeness closely match electronic nose use, with sensors detecting odour. The robot context differs.
Fingertip thermocouples are touch-like sensors, but the lie-detector function is quite different.
More sensory devices for judging facts is vague and unrelated to smell or touch specifically.
Fully automatic power machinery needing a few attendants matches a nearly unattended plant. The mechanism is not described.
Complete mass-production factories turning out ships continuously match automated production in function. The mining and transmutation details are fantastical.
A machine that adjusts all other machines from control-room orders matches automated plant control, though not a fully unattended plant.
Machines that run with no maintenance or attention match unattended operation in function, with no mechanism.
Fully automatic spare-parts factories that make a system self-sufficient match automated production, with no mechanism.
Machines working with no operator on site match unattended operation, but it is installation work, not a factory.
A cybernetic control system for reactors is automation of a plant, but safety control rather than unattended running.
A self-sustaining automated factory that builds and repairs robots with no supervision closely matches a robots-making-robots plant. The atomic pile and timespan differ.
Machines to run the machines is a vague gesture at self-maintaining automation.
A self-sustaining robot-operated station running without crew matches unattended operation, but it is a station rather than a factory.
Factory machines controlled by brain-analogue computers gesture at automation, but unattended running is not stated.
Machines controlled by computers copying a human mind are only loosely related to unattended factory automation.
One cybernetic brain controlling quality across all factories matches centralised automated plant control, though it is not stated to run without workers.
Gadgets that take care of themselves are a loose hint of self-running systems.
Self-maintaining caretaker islands are a loose analogue of self-maintaining plant.
An automated complex running outside human control points loosely at automated plant.
Robot controls that do the observers' work are partial automation, not a self-running plant.
A control panel for a power plant operated by a wired-in human is a loose fit, since it is not unattended.
Robot postal stations sorting mail in bulk match unattended automated processing in function. It is a postal plant rather than a factory.
Programmed heads producing completed modules in a near-continuous stream match automated manufacturing in function. Unattended running is not stated.
Automated equipment with failover channels is reliability for automation in general and not a plant running unattended.
A fully automated assembly line matches the function, with no mechanism or unattended detail.
A list of robot and machine-supervisor staff points loosely to automated plants with few workers.
Getting machines and robot workers is a loose gesture at automated production.
Entirely automatic stations needing no human match unattended plant operation in function. The mechanism is only 'cybernetic'.
An assembly-line process turning out a car every fifteen minutes is an inspection line and not a self-running plant.
Doors opening at a wave of the hand match automatic doors triggered by sensing a person. The mechanism is not described.
A conventional electric eye at the door matches sensor-triggered doors, though the point is the voice screening.
A panel sliding open on a photo-electronic trigger matches a sensor door. A ring key is the trigger, which differs from presence sensing.
A voice-identifying entry system is access control, not a sensor door that opens for approach.
Gates that recognise a person and open are access control by recognition, a loose match.
A door rising at a voice is an automatic door but with a voice trigger, not presence sensing.
A card-reading gate is access control. It is only loosely like a sensor door.
Body inductance triggers a butler that speaks. It is presence detection but it does not open a door.
Fingerprint-scanner door locks are identity access control, a loose match to sensor doors.
A door that opens to a spoken name is voice access control, a loose match.
A door opening to a whistled code word is voice-triggered, a loose match to sensor doors.
Crossing an electronic beam triggers a voice message. The beam is a sensor, but it does not open the door.
A scanner that identifies a person and opens the door is access control rather than a sensor door.
A door opening on a fingerprint imprint is biometric access control, a loose match.
A door opening to a thumb on an identity plate is biometric access control, a loose match.
A door that opens by itself without a visible photo-electric eye matches automatic opening on approach, though the voice identification differs.
A machine acting independently in response to its sensory inputs is loosely autopilot-like, but the quote does not describe flight control.
A helium brain with neuron-like circuits is a loosely evocative natural brain. It is not computing with biological molecules.
A brain built of condensers and relays is electronic, not biological, so it is not the same thing as a biological computer.
A glass-tube brain filled with nerve fluid is evocative of a wet biological computer, with nothing about computation.
A tubing brain activated by nerve fluid is loosely evocative of a biological computer.
A substance mixture that duplicates thinking and is used in calculators hints at chemical computing, but loosely.
A chemical nerve fluid that makes a brain work is only loosely like biomolecular computing.
A molecular chain reaction carrying impulses is molecular signalling, but it is not computing as in DNA computing.
A large mass of artificial brain tissue as an advisory store is a loose analogue of a biological computer.
A chemical goop that stores memory like a brain points at molecular information storage. It does not compute.
A part-organic artificial brain is in the direction of a biological computer, with no computing mechanism.
The quote only gives a brain-switching-operations number, so it is loose. The living computing component is evocative of a biological computer.
Human components in a machine that can reprogram themselves are a living-computer idea, but loosely.
A human turned into a control component of machinery is an evocative living-computer idea, not molecular computation.
A human used as a process controller sending binary signals is a loose living-computer idea.
Linked brains in a nutrient tank forming one computing unit match computing with living matter. The mechanism differs from DNA molecules.
Linked humans operating binary switches is a loose living-controller idea.
Organic compounds arranged as microscopic logic circuits match molecular computing in function. The mechanism is not stated to be DNA or biological.
Protoplasmic computers that plan operations match computing with organic matter in function, with no mechanism.
A synthetic brain with axons that degrade by mutation is loosely biological computing, with no computation described.
A tower housing a central brain is not described as biological computing or as anything close to the milestone.
